Video lab: title editor, cinema sound, wide gamut, timeline skin, WebGPU player

Five experiments with a <video> as a canvas child. The first three share one WebGL canvas: choose a scene with the buttons. In the editor, tap the text of a title card on the canvas and type. In the cinema, tap play on the screen, then tap a seat. The last two sections have their own canvases further down.

The controls on the screen in the room are the video's own and take taps there. The Play button here does the same as the one on the screen. Headphones make the position of the sound clearer. The yellow seat is the listener, and the arrow on it is the way the head faces.

Wide-gamut video in a Display P3 canvas

The same element (a video and three CSS swatches at the Display P3 primaries) is a child of two 2D canvases. The left context is sRGB and the right one is Display P3. On a wide-gamut screen the right canvas is more saturated. On any screen, "Read the pixels" reports the values and marks the pixels that sRGB can't hold.

The player shader in WebGPU

The shader of /player-fx/ in WGSL. The controls of the video are one texture and its frame is another. "Meld" draws the play button's glyph large as a lens over the frame while the video is paused: tap play to see it shrink into the button.

How it works

  • One WebGL context. The three scenes are sets of children of one canvas. A scene that isn't chosen has its elements hidden, so they aren't painted and take no taps. One fragment shader has a mode for each kind of quad.
  • Title editor. Each shot is an element the size of the canvas: a <video> in a wrapper, or a title card. At any time one or two shots are uploaded with texElementSubImage2D(). Where two overlap, the shader mixes them with the chosen transition. The shot in front has its hit box on the canvas, so a title card is edited in place.
  • Export. exportFrames() from lib/video-export.js seeks one video per frame. Here it is given an object with currentTime, pause() and a seeked event that seeks every video on the timeline and sets each card's --t. Each frame is one paint and one VideoFrame from the canvas.
  • Cinema screen. The screen, its reflection and the floor are three quads with perspective matrices. The same matrix, with the conversion to CSS pixels, goes to updateElementGeometry(), so the video's native controls and the seat buttons take taps where they are drawn. The page doesn't use three.js here: the site allows one WebGL context per page and the scenes share it.
  • Sound. createMediaElementSource(video) feeds a PannerNode at the centre of the screen. The AudioListener is at the chosen seat. The two meters are the level of each output channel, measured by two AnalyserNodes.
  • Timeline skin. For one paint, ::-webkit-media-controls-timeline gets a magenta background. That picture goes into a spare texture, the bottom quarter is read once, and the box of the magenta pixels is the timeline. The shader replaces the pixels inside the box and adds a glow at the playhead.
  • Wide gamut. The two canvases differ only in the colorSpace of their 2D context. Pixels are never read from them: each is copied with drawImage() into a plain canvas with the same colour space, and that copy is read with getImageData({ colorSpace: 'display-p3' }).
  • WebGPU player. GPUQueue.drawElementImageToTexture() uploads the controls. copyExternalImageToTexture() uploads the frame from the same video. The device comes from the page's shared webgpu(). Where that gives none, the player is drawn with the 2D context and no shader.

Live checks

The checks build their own small canvases in a corner of the window. The demos above aren't touched.

Findings

Measured in Chromium 157, headless, software rendering, on 2026-11-21. The rows above say what your browser does.

  • Works: video clips and HTML title cards as shots, with shader transitions. All five transitions start on the first shot and end on the second. Three of them are the GLSL of /transitions/, unchanged.
  • Works: a title card edited on a WebGL canvas. The card in front takes the tap, the caret and the typing.
  • Works: frame-by-frame export of several videos and cards. The exported file holds the frames that were asked for. It has no sound track: exportFrames() takes the sound of one video.
  • Works: native video controls and buttons on quads in perspective. elementFromPoint() returns the video at the projected centre of the screen and a seat button at its projected centre.
  • Works: a PannerNode at the screen. Rendered offline, a seat on the left hears more in the right ear and a seat near the screen hears more than one at the back.
  • Works: a shader on the timeline only. With the skin on and off, no pixel outside the strip and its glow changes.
  • Works: a wide-gamut video keeps its colours in a Display P3 canvas. The red of a BT.2020 clip reads as Display P3 (118, 0, 3) there and as (119, 21, 12) from the sRGB canvas. drawElementImage() and drawImage(video) give the same values.
  • Limit: an HDR10 video is tone-mapped to at most 1.0. In a float16 Display P3 canvas the brightest part of a PQ clip is 1.0, the same as in an 8-bit canvas.
  • Works off screen: the WGSL shader. On the software adapter the pass was rendered to a texture and read back. copyExternalImageToTexture(video) failed there, and the frame came through createImageBitmap(video).
  • Not verified: WebGPU on screen, an HDR screen, and the sound through real speakers. The test browser has none of them.
